entities.description:
Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. entities.description: Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

CT Scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a medical imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles and combining them with a computer to produce detailed three-dimensional (3-D) pictures, as well as cross-sectional images of tissues, organs, and other structures. These scans are often performed with the use of a contrast agent to enhance image clarity, particularly for cancer detection and evaluation.

CT scans are widely used in oncology for detecting tumors, identifying cancer spread (metastasis), and staging diseases. They are commonly employed to image the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to check if cancer has spread to organs such as the liver, lungs, or other areas. For specific conditions, such as rectal cancer, CT scans help assess spread to chest and abdominal organs, while in colon cancer, they are used for surveillance in stages 2 and 3. Additionally, CT imaging is useful for detecting cancer spread to lymph nodes and for guiding procedures like lymph node or other biopsies.

Beyond diagnostic and staging purposes, CT scans play a critical role in treatment planning. They are used during radiation therapy simulation to obtain precise pictures of the cancer site, which aids in creating an effective treatment plan. The technique is also considered an alternative imaging method when MRI is unavailable or not recommended, as CT scans are generally faster to perform than MRI scans. Overall, CT scans are a versatile and essential tool for diagnosing abnormalities, guiding interventions, and monitoring treatment outcomes.

Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures of the lymphatic system and integral components of the body’s immune system. Distributed throughout the body, they act as filters for lymph fluid and help fight infection. In the context of cancer, lymph nodes are significant because they can be primary sites of metastasis, where cancer cells spread from a primary tumor. Regional lymph nodes are those located near the tumor, and sentinel lymph nodes are specifically the first nodes to which cancer cells are expected to drain and spread. Cancer involvement in lymph nodes can cause them to swell, and this spread is often detected through imaging techniques such as PET/CT scans, as well as through biopsies. Because they are common sites of metastasis, lymph nodes are frequently biopsied to determine whether cancer has spread, which is a critical step in staging and treatment planning.

PET/CT Scan is a combined imaging modality that integrates Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and Computed Tomography (CT) into a single procedure. This fusion allows for the simultaneous acquisition of both functional and anatomical images, providing a comprehensive view of the body's internal structures and metabolic activity. The PET component typically involves the use of a radioactive drug (tracer) to highlight areas of high cellular activity, while the CT component produces detailed cross-sectional images of the body's anatomy. By merging these two data sets, the PET/CT Scan generates highly detailed, whole-body images that are particularly effective for detecting, localizing, and assessing the spread of cancer. This imaging technique is widely utilized in oncology, including specific applications such as evaluating prostate cancer, as it enables clinicians to identify cancer locations and determine whether the disease has metastasized to other parts of the body. entities.description: Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Adenocarcinoma is a broad category of cancer that originates in glandular cells, which are responsible for producing and secreting substances such as mucus. This cancer type can arise in various organs, and its characteristics and prevalence differ depending on the location. In the lungs, adenocarcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that begins in the mucus-making cells lining the alveoli. It is the most common subtype of NSCLC. In the colorectal region, adenocarcinoma is the most frequent type of tumor, forming within adenomas (precancerous polyps) and representing the most common form of both colon and rectal cancer. It also accounts for the vast majority of colorectal cancers overall, distinguishing it from cancers arising from squamous cells.

Adenocarcinoma also occurs in other parts of the digestive and reproductive systems. In the stomach, it is the most common type of cancer, developing from the mucus-secreting cells that line the stomach wall; indeed, nearly all stomach cancers are adenocarcinomas. In the cervix, adenocarcinoma is a recognized type of cervical cancer that arises from the glandular cells located in the endocervix, and it is considered a common form of this disease. Additionally, adenocarcinoma can appear in the bladder, where it is a less common, non-urothelial type of cancer. Across all these sites, the defining feature of adenocarcinoma is its origin in glandular tissue, which influences its behavior, diagnosis, and treatment.

The cervix is the lower part of the uterus that connects to the vagina, forming a key component of the female reproductive system. It is a narrow structure that plays a critical role in reproductive health, as it opens during childbirth to allow passage of the baby. Anatomically, the cervix is composed of two main regions: the ectocervix (the outer part visible during examination) and the endocervix (the inner canal leading to the uterus). 

Clinically, the cervix is a central focus in gynecological care. It is routinely examined during pelvic exams and sampled via a Pap test to screen for abnormalities, particularly cervical cancer, which originates in this tissue. The cervix is also a primary site for human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, a major risk factor for cancer development. In addition to screening, the cervix is involved in diagnostic and surgical procedures: it is the site where dye is injected for sentinel node biopsy, and it is removed during a hysterectomy or a trachelectomy (a fertility-sparing surgery). Overall, the cervix serves as both a structural gateway and a key area for cancer prevention and treatment.

Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Immunotherapy is a form of cancer treatment that leverages the body's own immune system to identify, target, and destroy cancer cells. It is classified as a systemic therapy, meaning it works throughout the body, and functions by either stimulating or re-activating the immune system's natural defenses against tumors. This approach can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments, and its application spans various cancer types, including recurrent ovarian cancer, advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, metastatic thyroid cancer, and primary CNS lymphoma, where the monoclonal antibody rituximab is a key agent.

A prominent and often preferred method within immunotherapy involves the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors, which include drugs that target proteins such as PD-1 and PD-L1. A specific example of this class is pembrolizumab. These inhibitors are frequently utilized in clinical practice, particularly for cancers like metastatic anal cancer, where they serve as a primary treatment or are recommended when the disease progresses during or after chemotherapy. In some cases, such as progressive anal cancer, these inhibitors may be administered before surgery. Additionally, immunotherapy can be delivered directly into the bladder for certain malignancies.

The application of immunotherapy is sometimes guided by the presence of specific biomarkers to determine patient eligibility. While it offers a powerful mechanism for fighting cancer, it is not without side effects. Potential adverse reactions include autoimmune responses, fatigue, fever, nausea, loss of appetite, infection, diarrhea, and constipation. Overall, immunotherapy represents a versatile and increasingly central strategy in oncology, offering options for both early and advanced-stage diseases across a wide spectrum of cancer types.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an alliance of cancer centers that develops and publishes expert recommendations and guidelines for cancer care. Its primary role is to provide evidence-based treatment guidelines, which are widely used by healthcare professionals to determine appropriate therapies, including chemotherapy regimens. NCCN also offers patient-specific guidelines and resources, making complex medical information accessible to individuals affected by cancer.

In addition to its clinical guidelines, NCCN provides patient education materials, including an app designed to deliver cancer information and assist with managing treatment side effects. The organization also facilitates patient feedback through surveys, which can be accessed via its website at NCCN.org/patients/feedback. These resources aim to support patients in understanding their diagnosis, treatment options, and care pathways, including referrals to specialized cancer centers and genetic counseling for individuals with inherited cancer syndromes.

Overall, NCCN functions as a comprehensive resource hub, bridging expert medical knowledge and patient support. Its dual focus on professional treatment standards and patient empowerment underscores its commitment to improving cancer care quality and patient experience across the continuum of care.

Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are a comprehensive set of patient-friendly guidelines published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), a nonprofit alliance of leading cancer centers. These guidelines translate the expert consensus of the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology into plain-language explanations, designed to help people with cancer, their families, and caregivers understand current care recommendations. The guidelines are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers, providing trusted, up-to-date information on cancer treatment, testing, staging, and side effects.

These resources cover a wide range of cancer types, including squamous cell skin cancer, melanoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, anal cancer, bone cancer, and certain lymphomas, as well as topics like adolescent and young adult cancer. They also address specific concerns such as immunotherapy side effects and fertility and family planning for cancer patients. The guidelines aim to empower patients to make informed, shared decisions with their care team by clearly explaining their treatment options and what to expect.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are accessible in multiple formats, including online at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and through the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. They are also available as printed books. The NCCN encourages users to provide feedback through surveys to help improve the guidelines. Overall, these guidelines serve as a vital educational resource, bridging the gap between complex medical information and patient understanding, ensuring individuals are well-informed participants in their own cancer care journey.

Beyond disease-specific guidance, the platform addresses supportive care topics, including the management of side effects from immune checkpoint inhibitors, strategies for managing nausea, and resources for coping with distress. Additionally, the website provides patient guidelines and resources aimed at cancer survivorship, making it a multifaceted tool for patients, caregivers, and individuals seeking reliable, expert-reviewed information throughout the cancer journey.

Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Detection and risk assessment involve various tests, including PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, biopsy, and grading, and the disease often requires staging and treatment. The condition is also a focus of risk assessment and genetic testing discussions, as it is characterized by the presence of prostate cancer cells and abnormal cell growth within the gland.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Patient is an individual receiving medical care, typically within the context of a suspected or confirmed cancer diagnosis, including specific types such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), mouth cancer, kidney cancer, breast cancer, and bone cancer. This person may be undergoing evaluation, diagnostic testing, medical imaging, and various medical procedures, and is actively engaged with a care team throughout the process. The patient may also be involved in breast cancer screening and other preventive or diagnostic measures.

In addition to receiving care, the patient is an active participant in their healthcare journey, often encouraged to advocate for themselves, ask questions, and engage in treatment planning. As someone diagnosed with cancer, the patient receives medical advice and is involved in making informed treatment decisions. Overall, the patient is the central individual undergoing tests, interacting with healthcare providers, and receiving comprehensive care tailored to their specific condition.

Adenocarcinoma is a broad category of cancer that originates in glandular cells, which are responsible for producing and secreting substances such as mucus. This cancer type can arise in various organs, and its characteristics and prevalence differ depending on the location. In the lungs, adenocarcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that begins in the mucus-making cells lining the alveoli. It is the most common subtype of NSCLC. In the colorectal region, adenocarcinoma is the most frequent type of tumor, forming within adenomas (precancerous polyps) and representing the most common form of both colon and rectal cancer. It also accounts for the vast majority of colorectal cancers overall, distinguishing it from cancers arising from squamous cells.

Adenocarcinoma also occurs in other parts of the digestive and reproductive systems. In the stomach, it is the most common type of cancer, developing from the mucus-secreting cells that line the stomach wall; indeed, nearly all stomach cancers are adenocarcinomas. In the cervix, adenocarcinoma is a recognized type of cervical cancer that arises from the glandular cells located in the endocervix, and it is considered a common form of this disease. Additionally, adenocarcinoma can appear in the bladder, where it is a less common, non-urothelial type of cancer. Across all these sites, the defining feature of adenocarcinoma is its origin in glandular tissue, which influences its behavior, diagnosis, and treatment.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Primary Tumor refers to the original mass of cancer cells formed at the site where cancer first began, distinguishing it from secondary growths or metastases. It is the initial tumor and the main area of cancer growth, serving as the primary reference point for staging the extent of the disease. The TNM System is a standardized cancer staging system used to describe the anatomical extent of a malignant disease. It evaluates three key components: the primary tumor (T), the involvement of regional lymph nodes (N), and the presence of distant metastasis (M). These categories are assessed and combined to assign an overall cancer stage, which helps guide prognosis and treatment decisions.

This system is applied across various cancer types, including mouth cancer, throat cancer, and most bone cancers. For each specific cancer, the T, N, and M scores are defined to reflect the unique patterns of local growth, lymphatic spread, and distant dissemination. The TNM System provides a common language for clinicians to describe tumor size, extent of spread, and the presence of secondary growths, ensuring consistent and objective disease classification.

Blood is a specialized bodily fluid and tissue that circulates throughout the body, playing essential roles in transporting oxygen and nutrients to cells while carrying away metabolic waste products. It is composed of plasma and formed elements, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Beyond transport, blood is integral to the immune system, defending against pathogens, and to hemostasis, preventing bleeding through clotting mechanisms. Blood also serves as a conduit for hormones, facilitating endocrine signaling, and can be a vehicle for the spread of cancer cells during metastasis, as seen in conditions like liver cancer.

In clinical and diagnostic contexts, blood is a versatile sample source. It is used for genetic testing, including mutation and predisposition testing, as well as tumor marker tests. For certain procedures, such as karyotyping, a blood sample (or bone marrow) is required because it provides living cells that can be cultured and grown. Blood is also a critical medium for monitoring hematologic malignancies; for instance, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), it may contain an accumulation of immature blasts, while in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the overproduction of lymphoblasts can crowd out normal blood cell production. Additionally, blood can harbor cancer cells or circulating tumor DNA, making it a key specimen for liquid biopsies. In therapeutic contexts, blood is a source for harvesting stem cells, which can be used in transplantation and regenerative treatments.

Care Team is a group of healthcare professionals involved in a patient's care, diagnosis, and treatment. This multidisciplinary team typically includes doctors, nurses, specialists, technicians, and therapists, and may also encompass psychosocial care professionals. The composition of the team can vary depending on the patient's condition; for example, in oncology settings, it is specifically focused on cancer care, while for conditions like Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML), it is a multidisciplinary team that plans and implements treatment.

The Care Team is responsible for a range of clinical activities, including assessing the patient, interpreting imaging results, using staging and grading to predict disease course, planning treatment, and making treatment decisions. They also manage patient allergies and discuss results among themselves. Beyond direct clinical duties, the team serves as a key point of contact for the patient, providing care and information, and maintaining updated contact information is considered important for communication. The team collectively plans and manages the patient's care, deciding on next steps in the treatment process.

Head And Neck Cancer is a broad and diverse category of malignancies that arise in the squamous cells lining the mucosal surfaces of the head and neck region. This group encompasses cancers of the oral cavity (including the mouth, jaw, teeth, and gums), the pharynx (throat), the larynx (voice box), and associated glands. As a broader classification, it includes specific subtypes such as throat cancer. The primary risk factors for developing these cancers include the use of tobacco and alcohol, though a subset of these cancers is also caused by the Human Papillomavirus (HPV).

The disease and its treatment can have significant impacts on a patient's quality of life, potentially affecting the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, and may necessitate dental work prior to the initiation of treatment. Furthermore, cancer therapies for this region can impact fertility. For patients, particularly those with smoking or vaping habits, cessation is deemed essential to maximize the chances of a cure and to minimize the severity of treatment-related side effects.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Fertility is the ability to conceive or have children, a consideration that applies to individuals of all genders. In the context of cancer care, fertility is a significant health concern because cancer treatments—including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and other modalities—can adversely affect a person’s reproductive capacity. This impact is relevant across various cancer types, such as follicular lymphoma, head and neck cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and anal cancer, among others.

For patients, fertility is an important topic to discuss with their healthcare team before and during treatment planning. Such discussions allow for proactive measures, including fertility testing for all genders, to assess and preserve reproductive potential. The potential for treatment-related infertility means that fertility considerations should be integrated into the overall care strategy, ensuring patients are informed about risks and available options. Across different cancer diagnoses, the core message remains consistent: cancer treatment may affect fertility, and addressing this concern is a vital part of comprehensive patient care.

Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

Fertility preservation refers to the range of actions, methods, and processes undertaken to safeguard a person’s ability to have biological children in the future, most commonly discussed and implemented before cancer treatment that may impair fertility. This practice is centered on keeping reproductive options open for later in life, particularly for patients who are at risk of infertility due to medical interventions such as chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. The core objective is to protect or save eggs, sperm, or reproductive tissue so that individuals can potentially conceive biological children after their treatment concludes.

The specific techniques involved in fertility preservation include the collection and freezing of sperm or eggs, as well as more advanced procedures such as ovarian tissue banking and ovarian transposition. These methods are designed to enable future pregnancy by preserving reproductive cells or tissues prior to the start of cancer therapy. The process is typically discussed with patients before they begin treatment, ensuring that they are informed of their options and can make proactive decisions about their reproductive health. While the primary context is cancer care, the underlying principle of fertility preservation is broadly applicable to anyone seeking to maintain the possibility of having children later in life, whether due to medical reasons or personal choice.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

The liver is a large organ located in the abdomen, on the right side of the body under the rib cage, and is a central component of the digestive system. It performs numerous vital functions, including filtering blood to remove toxins, producing bile to break down fats, processing nutrients and sugar for energy, synthesizing coagulation factors to aid in blood clotting, and producing lymph. Its health and function are commonly assessed through blood tests, such as a chemistry profile or liver function tests, and it can be imaged using MRI to detect signs of disease.

The liver is a frequent and clinically significant site for cancer metastasis. It is a common destination for cancer cells originating from various primary tumors, including breast, colon, rectal, anal, stomach, pancreatic, cervical, bladder, kidney, prostate, throat, and nasopharyngeal cancers. In many of these cases, such as with colon cancer, the liver is a primary site for stage 4 spread, while for others, like kidney cancer, it is a less frequent but still possible site of distant metastasis. The liver can also be affected by leukemia spreading outside the bloodstream, and cancer cell buildup in the organ can cause it to swell.

Beyond its role in metastasis, the liver is susceptible to damage from certain medical treatments, such as high-dose methotrexate. As an organ that processes chemicals, its function is critical to overall health, and its assessment is a standard part of medical diagnostics.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are a comprehensive set of patient-friendly guidelines published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), a nonprofit alliance of leading cancer centers. These guidelines translate the expert consensus of the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology into plain-language explanations, designed to help people with cancer, their families, and caregivers understand current care recommendations. The guidelines are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers, providing trusted, up-to-date information on cancer treatment, testing, staging, and side effects.

These resources cover a wide range of cancer types, including squamous cell skin cancer, melanoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, anal cancer, bone cancer, and certain lymphomas, as well as topics like adolescent and young adult cancer. They also address specific concerns such as immunotherapy side effects and fertility and family planning for cancer patients. The guidelines aim to empower patients to make informed, shared decisions with their care team by clearly explaining their treatment options and what to expect.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are accessible in multiple formats, including online at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and through the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. They are also available as printed books. The NCCN encourages users to provide feedback through surveys to help improve the guidelines. Overall, these guidelines serve as a vital educational resource, bridging the gap between complex medical information and patient understanding, ensuring individuals are well-informed participants in their own cancer care journey.

The lungs are a pair of organs located in the chest, forming a critical component of the respiratory system. Their primary physiological function is to facilitate gas exchange, moving oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of it, and they are the essential organs responsible for breathing. Beyond their normal function, the lungs are a significant clinical focus in oncology, serving as a frequent and common site for distant metastasis for numerous primary cancers. Specifically, they are a well-documented destination for cancer spread from the throat, rectum, kidney, pancreas, prostate, breast, colon, cervix, stomach, bladder, and anus. In the context of specific cancers, the lungs are a common site for metastasis in stage 4 colon cancer, a potential site for spread in nasopharyngeal and stomach cancers, and a frequent target for metastatic cervical, anal, and pancreatic cancers. Additionally, the lungs are the primary site where small cell lung cancer (SCLC) tumors can grow and spread. Due to their susceptibility to metastatic involvement, the lungs are routinely examined via chest imaging to detect potential cancer spread. While they are a common metastatic target for many malignancies, they are also an organ to which cancer cells less frequently spread in certain other contexts.

Adenocarcinoma is a broad category of cancer that originates in glandular cells, which are responsible for producing and secreting substances such as mucus. This cancer type can arise in various organs, and its characteristics and prevalence differ depending on the location. In the lungs, adenocarcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that begins in the mucus-making cells lining the alveoli. It is the most common subtype of NSCLC. In the colorectal region, adenocarcinoma is the most frequent type of tumor, forming within adenomas (precancerous polyps) and representing the most common form of both colon and rectal cancer. It also accounts for the vast majority of colorectal cancers overall, distinguishing it from cancers arising from squamous cells.

Adenocarcinoma also occurs in other parts of the digestive and reproductive systems. In the stomach, it is the most common type of cancer, developing from the mucus-secreting cells that line the stomach wall; indeed, nearly all stomach cancers are adenocarcinomas. In the cervix, adenocarcinoma is a recognized type of cervical cancer that arises from the glandular cells located in the endocervix, and it is considered a common form of this disease. Additionally, adenocarcinoma can appear in the bladder, where it is a less common, non-urothelial type of cancer. Across all these sites, the defining feature of adenocarcinoma is its origin in glandular tissue, which influences its behavior, diagnosis, and treatment.

entities.description: Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

The liver is a large organ located in the abdomen, on the right side of the body under the rib cage, and is a central component of the digestive system. It performs numerous vital functions, including filtering blood to remove toxins, producing bile to break down fats, processing nutrients and sugar for energy, synthesizing coagulation factors to aid in blood clotting, and producing lymph. Its health and function are commonly assessed through blood tests, such as a chemistry profile or liver function tests, and it can be imaged using MRI to detect signs of disease.

The liver is a frequent and clinically significant site for cancer metastasis. It is a common destination for cancer cells originating from various primary tumors, including breast, colon, rectal, anal, stomach, pancreatic, cervical, bladder, kidney, prostate, throat, and nasopharyngeal cancers. In many of these cases, such as with colon cancer, the liver is a primary site for stage 4 spread, while for others, like kidney cancer, it is a less frequent but still possible site of distant metastasis. The liver can also be affected by leukemia spreading outside the bloodstream, and cancer cell buildup in the organ can cause it to swell.

Beyond its role in metastasis, the liver is susceptible to damage from certain medical treatments, such as high-dose methotrexate. As an organ that processes chemicals, its function is critical to overall health, and its assessment is a standard part of medical diagnostics.

Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Detection and risk assessment involve various tests, including PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, biopsy, and grading, and the disease often requires staging and treatment. The condition is also a focus of risk assessment and genetic testing discussions, as it is characterized by the presence of prostate cancer cells and abnormal cell growth within the gland.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Metastasis is the biological process by which cancer spreads from its primary, or original, site to other parts of the body. This dissemination occurs when cancer cells travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system, enabling them to establish new tumors in distant or nearby anatomical locations. The process is a defining characteristic of advanced-stage cancer, as it marks the transition from a localized disease to a systemic one.

The specific destinations for metastatic spread vary depending on the origin of the primary cancer. Common sites of secondary tumor formation include the lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and liver. For instance, metastasis from prostate cancer defines advanced-stage disease, while bladder cancer may spread to lymph nodes, bones, liver, or lungs. In the context of kidney cancer, metastasis refers to the formation of new tumors outside the kidney itself.

Clinically, the presence of metastasis often necessitates further diagnostic procedures, such as a biopsy, to confirm the spread and guide treatment decisions. The formation of these secondary tumors is a critical factor in cancer prognosis, as it indicates that the disease has become more complex and challenging to treat.

For prostate cancer, germline testing looks for characteristic changes in these genes: BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, and others. Some mutations can put you at risk for more than one type of cancer. Germline mutations in genes like BRCA1 or BRCA2 are also related to breast cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, and skin cancer (melanoma). Germline mutations in MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2 are related to colorectal and uterine cancers in addition to prostate cancer. If a germline mutation is suspected based on your family’s or your own health history, you should ask about testing. Your doctor can talk to you about testing or refer you to a genetic counselor. A genetic counselor is an expert who has special training in genetic diseases. A genetic counselor can help you decide whether you would like to undergo germline testing and help you interpret the results of these tests. Germline testing is recommended for those with prostate cancer and any of the following: Family members or relatives who have or had prostate cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, intestinal cancer, and certain other cancers Family history of mutations in certain genes including BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, and others High-risk, very-high-risk, regional, or metastatic prostate cancer regardless of family history Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry Having any other type of cancer Talk to your medical providers and/or a genetic counselor about your family history of cancer. Molecular biomarker testing In biomarker testing, a sample from your biopsy is tested to look at its molecular components. This information helps figure out how likely your cancer could spread to other parts of the body. Biomarker testing can be considered for those with localized, regional, or metastatic prostate cancer. Biomarker testing is sometimes called genomic testing, tumor profiling, or molecular tumor testing. The main reason to have a molecular biomarker test is to help assess whether you have lower risk or higher risk prostate cancer. If you have lower risk cancer, you may be able to avoid or delay treatment such as surgery or radiation therapy, which means you’d also avoid or delay any treatment-related complications and side effects. At the same time, a molecular biomarker test can flag those who have higher risk prostate cancer, which may give them a head start on treatment. After being told you have cancer, your next thought may be, “How soon can I start treatment to get rid of it?” The fact is, a lot of patients with early-stage prostate cancer don’t need treatment right away. Many never need treatment. Figuring out whether someone needs treatment and which treatment to use requires an assessment of their risks. A risk assessment is a process for identifying potential problems and then considering what would happen if those problems occurred. In the case of early-stage prostate cancer, a risk assessment considers how likely the cancer is to remain within the prostate or to spread to outside the prostate. A risk assessment also considers whether the cancer may come back after treatment (recurrence) and, if so, whether it can be controlled with a different type of treatment. To assess risk, your care providers use these tools: risk groups, life expectancy, nomograms, and molecular biomarker tests. Because your risk group is the basis for your prognosis. A prognosis predicts the likely course and outcome of a disease. Your prognosis guides your treatment options. For example, patients with lower risk generally get minimal treatment or no treatment at all. Patients with higher risk usually get more aggressive treatment. Nutritional and digestive tract health Your provider may ask about your diet and eating habits. Symptoms of ovarian cancer include bloating, pain in the pelvis or abdomen, difficulty eating, and feeling full quickly. These symptoms may cause you to eat less in general, or to eat foods lacking in nutrients. Your overall health and nutrition level can have an impact on the success of surgery and other treatment outcomes. If you need help planning healthy meals or have questions about your diet, ask your provider for a referral to a registered dietitian or nutritionist. Your doctor may want to check your gastrointestinal (GI) tract using an imaging test. The GI tract is made of the organs that food passes through when you eat. This includes your stomach, small bowel, and large bowel (rectum and colon). An imaging tool called a scope is used to examine these organs. A scope is a long, thin tube with a light and a camera that can be guided into your body. A colonoscopy is used to examine the large bowel. This involves inserting a scope into your anus and guiding it through the rectum and colon. To examine the upper GI tract, a scope is guided down the throat into the esophagus, stomach, and small bowel. This is called an upper endoscopy. Blood tests The following tests are not used alone to diagnose ovarian cancer, but abnormal results may signal health problems. General health A complete blood count (CBC) measures the number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in a sample of blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen throughout the body. White blood cells fight infection. Platelets help to control bleeding. Your blood counts may be too low or too high because of cancer or other health problems. A blood chemistry profile measures the levels of different chemicals that are affected by your kidneys, bones, and other organs and tissues. Levels that are too high or too low may be a sign that an organ isn’t working well. Abnormal levels may also be caused by the spread of cancer or by other diseases. This test can also provide information about nutrient intake, such as protein levels. This can help guide treatment decisions. The liver is an organ that does many important jobs, such as removing toxins from your blood. Liver function tests measure chemicals that are made or processed by the liver. Levels that are too high or low may be a sign of liver damage or cancer spread. Tumor markers A tumor marker is a substance found in body tissue or fluid that may be a sign of cancer. Along with other information, tumor markers can help diagnose ovarian cancer and monitor response to treatment. A cancer antigen-125 (CA-125) test is the most common tumor marker test for ovarian cancer. High levels of this protein in the blood may be a sign of ovarian or other cancers. A CA-125 test alone cannot diagnose ovarian cancer. Health problems that are not cancer, such as endometriosis and diverticulitis, can raise your CA-125 level. Some ovarian cancers don’t cause CA-125 to rise. Your blood may also be tested for the following tumor markers. They are often mutations (changes) in the DNA of the cancer cells. Testing for biomarkers involves analyzing a piece of tumor tissue in a lab or testing a sample of blood. The results can be used to determine whether you can join certain clinical trials, and whether you may benefit from specific maintenance therapies. Other names for biomarker testing include molecular testing, tumor profiling, genomic testing, tumor gene testing, next-generation sequencing (NGS), mutation testing, liquid biopsy, and precision oncology. BRCA and HRD A BRCA mutation is the most important biomarker used to plan ovarian cancer treatment. Everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer should have the tumor tested for mutations in the BRCA genes, and in other similar genes important in DNA repair. This is different than genetic testing of the blood for inherited (germline) BRCA mutations. Mutations in the tumor itself are known as somatic or simply “tumor” mutations. BRCA mutations are a form of homologous recombination deficiency (HRD). This means that if you have a BRCA mutation, the cancer is also homologous recombination deficient or HRD positive. However, you can also have an HRD-positive tumor without a BRCA mutation. Other changes in the tumor’s DNA can make it homologous recombination deficient. The tumor's BRCA and HRD status are used to guide decisions about maintenance therapy after initial treatment. Other biomarkers The timing of testing for the biomarkers described next can vary. However, testing for these biomarkers is generally recommended for ovarian cancer that returns after treatment (recurrent). Testing is performed on removed tumor tissue. Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Detection and risk assessment involve various tests, including PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, biopsy, and grading, and the disease often requires staging and treatment. The condition is also a focus of risk assessment and genetic testing discussions, as it is characterized by the presence of prostate cancer cells and abnormal cell growth within the gland.
