contexts: just for you. First, they will need to gather information about the cancer and your general health. This chapter describes testing and other care needed to create your treatment plan. Biopsy Cervical biopsy and pathologic review A cervical biopsy involves removing small samples of tissue from the cervix. It is the most commonly used procedure to diagnose cervical cancer. Samples may be taken from the rounded, bottom part of the cervix (ectocervix) and/or from the endocervical canal. The removed tissue is examined by a specialized doctor called a pathologist. A pathologist is a doctor who specializes in evaluating cells and tissues to diagnose disease. The pathologist looks for abnormal areas, including areas of cancer or pre-cancer. The pathologist also determines the type of cervical cancer, when possible. Cone biopsy Cone biopsy can be both a test and a treatment. It may be used to gather more information about the extent of the cancer after a cervical biopsy. It is also a recommended treatment option for some early cervical cancers. Also known as cervical conization, cone biopsy involves removing a cone-shaped portion of the cervix. The cone-shaped sample includes tissue from both the ectocervix and the endocervical canal. All of the transformation zone—where the ectocervix and endocervix meet—is removed. Most cervical cancers start in this area. Most commonly, a technique called cold knife conization (CKC) is used. In this method a surgical scalpel is used to remove the tissue. In some cases loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) may be performed instead. In LEEP, a thin loop of electrified (heated) wire is used instead of a scalpel to cut out the cervical tissue. After removing the cone-shaped sample of tissue, your doctor may use a spoon-shaped tool called a curette to scrape a sample of tissue from the cervical canal. This is called endocervical curettage. The tissue removed during a cone biopsy is examined under a microscope by a pathologist. Cone biopsy A cone biopsy removes a coneshaped section of the cervix that includes the transformation zone. Cone biopsy may be the only treatment needed for some earlystage cervical cancers. Health history and physical exam To help plan treatment, expect your doctor to ask about your past and current health, including: Illnesses, diseases, and surgeries Medicines that you take (prescription or over-the-counter) Your lifestyle (your diet, activity level, whether you smoke or drink alcohol) Possible symptoms of cervical cancer, such as watery vaginal discharge Your doctor will also do a physical exam of your body, which may include: Checking your vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate, and body temperature) and overall appearance Feeling and/or listening to the organs in your abdomen, including your liver and stomach h A pelvic examination to check the size, position, and appearance of your cervix and uterus It is important to let your doctor know if you have trouble with pelvic exams due to pain, anxiety, or other reasons. Blood tests The following blood tests may be ordered as part of initial testing. They can provide helpful information about your general health and the health of your liver, kidneys, and other organs before treatment. A complete blood count (CBC) is a common test that measures the number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in a sample of blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen throughout the body. White blood cells fight infection. Platelets help to control bleeding. A blood chemistry profile measures the levels of different chemicals in your blood. Chemicals in your blood are affected by your kidneys, bones, and other organs and tissues. Blood chemistry levels that are too high or too low may be a sign that an organ is not working well. Abnormal levels may also be caused by the spread of cancer or by other diseases. Liver function tests are often done along with a blood chemistry profile. The liver is an organ that does many important jobs, such as remove toxins from the blood. Liver function tests measure enzymes that are made or processed by the liver. Levels that are too high or too low may be a sign of liver damage or cancer spread. If you have not had a recent human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test, or have never been tested, your doctor may recommend it. If you have HIV, you are likely to be referred to an HIV specialist. Having HIV should not affect your cancer treatment. The treatment options described in this guide apply to both HIV-positive and HIV-negative patients. Imaging Imaging helps determine the extent of the cancer. The size and spread of the cancer is used to guide treatment. Computed tomography You may have a computed tomography (CT) scan of your chest, abdomen, and/or pelvis. A CT scan is a more detailed kind of x-ray. It takes many pictures of an area inside the body from different angles. A computer combines the pictures to make three-dimensional (3-D) images. During the scan, you will lie face up on a table that moves through a large tunnel-like machine. To see everything better, a substance called contrast may be injected into your vein and also mixed with a liquid you drink. Contrast makes the CT pictures clearer. The contrast may cause you to feel flushed or get hives. You will be able to hear and talk to the technician at all times. You may hear buzzing or clicking during the scan. PET/CT A CT scan may be combined with another imaging test called positron emission tomography (PET). PET uses small amounts of radioactive materials called radiotracers. About an hour before the scan, you will be injected with a sugar radiotracer. The radiotracer gives off a small amount of energy that can be seen by the imaging machine. Cancer appears brighter in the pictures because cancer cells use sugar more quickly than normal cells. In some cases, PET may be performed with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

a patient’s pelvis. The greenish circle identifies cancer in the prostate, while the intense red dot indicates cancer that has spread to a pelvic lymph node. A special camera will take pictures of the tracer in your bones. Areas of bone damage absorb more tracer than healthy bone. These areas show up as bright spots in the pictures. Bone damage can be caused by cancer, cancer treatment, or other health problems. Biopsy Although a high PSA level and an abnormal digital rectal exam are signs of possible prostate cancer, the only way to confirm cancer is to have a biopsy. A biopsy is a procedure in which a sample of cells or tissue is removed from your body and tested for cancer. A biopsy is an invasive test, which means that it goes into (invades) your body. All invasive tests have some risk. The risks for a prostate biopsy include infection, bleeding, and pain. Doctors use invasive tests only when needed. You and your doctors will decide when, or if, you need a biopsy. A biopsy procedure is usually performed by a urologist. A urologist is a doctor who’s an expert in treating diseases of the urinary system and the male reproductive organs. For this procedure, you’ll lie on your side with your knees curled up or you’ll lie on your back with your legs raised. You’ll be given anesthesia to numb the pain or to put you to sleep. The urologist will insert a lubricated probe into your rectum. The probe provides a visual image of the prostate. The urologist will then insert a hollow needle into the prostate gland using the video display to guide it. The needle will be inserted either through the rectum or through the perineum (the skin between the anus and scrotum). When the urologist removes the needle, it will pull out a small sample of prostate tissue called a core. This is a transperineal biopsy, in which a needle is inserted through the perineum and into the prostate. The urologist will typically take 12 or more core samples from different parts of the prostate. Checking different areas provides a more complete evaluation of cancer throughout the gland. After the biopsy samples are removed, they’ll be sent to a lab for testing. At the lab, a specialist called a pathologist will examine the samples under a microscope and test them for cancer. The pathologist will find out how many of the core samples contain cancer and will also measure the percentage of cancer in each core. With this information, the pathologist can estimate the amount of cancer in the prostate. Also, by knowing where each core sample was taken, the pathologist can tell if the cancer is concentrated in a certain section of the prostate. The pathologist will put these results into a report. Ask your doctor to review the pathology report with you. It’s common to have more than one biopsy if you’re on active surveillance. You’ll have one biopsy to determine your diagnosis and another biopsy within a year (called a confirmatory biopsy) to see if any changes have happened over time. Having a biopsy may cause complications. A complication is an unwanted and unplanned result from a procedure. Complications may include infection, bleeding from the rectum, or blood in the urine, stool, or semen. These usually go away after a few days or, with semen, after a few weeks. However, it’s important to know that a biopsy doesn’t cause prostate cancer to spread or worsen. Genetic tests A genetic test is used to find abnormal changes in your genes. Genes are small segments of DNA inside every cell. Genes provide the instructions to tell the cell how to make proteins, which carry out a lot of important functions in the body. Once in a while, a gene will have or develop an abnormal change (mutation). A mutation is when something is different in your genes than in most other people’s genes. Sometimes an abnormal change can cause a gene to make the wrong type of protein or make no protein at all. This abnormality could affect the cell, which may in turn cause a disease such as cancer. Mutations can be passed down in families, in which case they occur in every cell in your body. Or mutations can occur spontaneously in just some of your cells. In other words, they may be present before you’re born (called an inherited or germline mutation) or occur on their own later in life (called an acquired or somatic mutation). The two basic types of genetic tests used for prostate cancer care are germline testing and molecular biomarker testing: Germline testing Sometimes, mutations in genes inherited from your parents can increase the risk of different cancers. You can pass these genes on to your children. Other family members might also carry these mutations. If you have a family history of cancer, your doctor might suggest genetic germline testing to find out if you have an inherited cancer risk. The goal of this type of genetic testing is to look for germline (inherited) mutations that occur in every cell in your body. Blood Tests are laboratory procedures performed on samples of blood to evaluate a patient’s overall health, detect abnormalities, and assess organ function. These medical tests are frequently documented in medical records and binders, serving as a foundational tool for diagnosing and monitoring a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. By analyzing blood components and chemicals, these tests can reveal signs of disease, measure how well organs are working, and identify specific markers or irregularities that guide clinical decision-making.

In the context of oncology, Blood Tests play a critical role across multiple cancer types. They are routine in cases of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), where results may be abnormal, and are integral to the diagnostic workup for esophageal cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma, where results help guide treatment plans. For suspected ovarian cancer, tests typically include a complete blood count (CBC), chemistry profile, liver function tests, and tumor marker tests. Similarly, for pancreatic cancer, these tests aid in diagnosis and management, while for primary CNS lymphoma, they help assess the condition. In leukemias like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), blood tests are used to diagnose, monitor, and direct treatment strategies. For thyroid cancer, they measure specific substances such as TSH, thyroglobulin (Tg), and Tg antibodies to track disease status.

Beyond initial diagnosis, Blood Tests are essential for ongoing patient care. They are ordered as needed to monitor health and cancer status during chemotherapy, and they help establish the extent of cancer spread for treatment planning. Specific tests, including CBC, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and liver function tests, are used to check for cancer recurrence and to evaluate organ function over time. Additionally, these tests are part of general health checks and are crucial for diagnosing and planning treatment for liver cancer. Overall, Blood Tests provide objective data on blood markers and health indicators, making them indispensable for detecting disease, assessing organ performance, and guiding therapeutic decisions across numerous medical scenarios.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.
A physical examination of the female reproductive organs, including the ovaries, cervix, and uterus.

Cancer Stage is a medical classification that describes the extent of cancer in the body, often written with Roman numerals (e.g., I, II, III, IV). It serves as a standardized assessment of how far the cancer has likely spread from its original site, such as the ovary, and is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment plan for a patient. The staging system categorizes the disease based on whether cancer has remained localized or has metastasized; specifically, stages I, II, and III are considered non-metastatic, indicating that the cancer is confined to the primary site or has spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes, while stage IV denotes metastatic cancer, meaning it has spread to distant organs or parts of the body. This classification provides a clear framework for healthcare providers to evaluate the severity of the disease, guide therapeutic decisions, and communicate the prognosis, ensuring that the treatment approach is tailored to the specific progression of the cancer.

Sarcomas Most primary bone cancers are sarcomas. Sarcomas are a rare group of cancers. There are 2 main types of sarcomas: Soft tissue sarcomas Bone sarcomas Soft tissue includes fat, muscles, nerves, tendons, blood and lymph vessels, and other supportive tissues of the body. Soft tissue sarcomas are more common than bone sarcomas. Bone sarcomas, such as osteosarcomas, start in the cells that form NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Bone Cancer, 2025 bone. Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and chondrosarcoma are the most common types of bone cancer, except multiple myeloma. For more information, see NCCN Guidelines for Patients®: Soft Tissue Sarcoma and NCCN Guidelines for Patients®: Multiple Myeloma at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Types of bone tumors A bone tumor is an abnormal growth of cells within a bone. A bone tumor may be cancerous (malignant) or noncancerous (benign). Bone tumors often occur in areas of the bone that grow rapidly (the metaphysis). This book will discuss the following: Chondrosarcoma – starts in the cells that form cartilage. Cartilage is a tough, flexible tissue that covers the ends of bones to form a smooth surface that makes a joint. Also, cartilage gives structure to the nose, ears, larynx, and other parts of the body. Chordoma – starts in notochordal cells that form the spine and vertebrae. Chordomas are usually found in the lower spinal column (sacrum) or at the base of the skull. Ewing sarcoma – starts in the bone marrow and commonly occurs in the diaphysis of long bones or flat bones like the pelvis or scapula (shoulder blade). Giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB) – is an overgrowth of cells found in the part of the bone called the metaphysis and extends into the area of the bone that widens to form a joint (epiphysis). Osteosarcoma – starts in cells most commonly in the areas of the bone that grow rapidly (metaphysis), near the growth plates. What is bone? Bone is a living tissue made up of specialized bone cells and collagen. Collagen is the most abundant protein in the body. Bone tissue also contains blood vessels, nerves, proteins, vitamins, and minerals. Bone is made up of the following: Compact bone or cortical bone – the hard, dense outer layer of bone that is covered by a membrane of strong connective tissue called the periosteum Spongey bone or cancellous bone – the spongy, porous inner layer of bone that contains red marrow Bone marrow – found in the center of most bones and has many blood vessels There are 2 types of bone marrow: red and yellow. Red marrow contains blood stem cells that can become red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets. Yellow marrow is made mostly of fat. Red marrow is often replaced by yellow marrow as we age. Why you should read this book Making decisions about cancer care can be stressful. You may need to make tough decisions under pressure about complex choices. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are trusted by patients and providers. They clearly explain current care recommendations made by respected experts in the field. Recommendations are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers. Cancer care is not the same for everyone. By following expert recommendations for your situation, you are more likely to improve your care and have better outcomes as a result. Use this book as your guide to find the information you need to make important decisions. Our body has 206 bones. Bones provide structure and support, protect our organs, create blood cells, store chemicals the body needs, and produce hormones. Bone is light, yet strong and can regrow. What's in this book? Chapter 3: Bone cancer staging explains how bone cancer is staged and where bone tumors might be found in the body. Chapter 4: Types of treatment gives an overview

. The level is checked to learn if the nodule is producing thyroid hormone. Nodules that make thyroid hormone are rarely cancerous. A high TSH level usually means that the thyroid hormone levels are low. A low TSH level usually means that the thyroid hormone levels are high. This is called hyperthyroidism or overactive thyroid. Your provider may order a radioactive iodine (RAI) uptake test. Ultrasound Ultrasound is the most common imaging technique used to look for thyroid cancer. It uses sound waves to form images showing the size, shape, and location of a thyroid nodule. An ultrasound of the thyroid and neck is brief and painless. It is usually done lying down. A Ultrasound An ultrasound of the thyroid and neck is one of the first tests ordered if a thyroid nodule is known or suspected. hand-held device called an ultrasound probe is used. After a gel is applied to the skin, the probe is moved back and forth over the thyroid area. If ultrasound finds any suspicious lymph nodes in the neck, further imaging with CT or MRI is recommended. A substance called contrast is used to make the pictures clearer. Biopsy A biopsy removes samples of fluid or tissue from the body to be tested. Your doctor will consider the nodule size and other features as seen on the ultrasound to determine if a biopsy is needed. Some nodules don't need to be biopsied and are monitored with ultrasound. If a biopsy is needed, fine-needle aspiration (also called needle biopsy or FNA) is recommended. This method uses a thin needle to take small samples of suspicious thyroid nodules. Ultrasound is usually done at the same time to help pinpoint the suspicious areas. Pathology review The biopsy samples are sent to a pathologist. Pathologists are physicians with expertise in examining tissues and cells to diagnose disease. By examining the sample under a microscope, the pathologist is able to determine whether the nodule is cancerous, and if so, the cancer type. In certain types of lesions, such as follicular and oncocytic tumors, fine-needle biopsy can identify the nature of the cells, but can't determine if the nodule is cancerous. For these lesions, surgery is often needed to make a final diagnosis. Now, molecular tests are available that can help determine whether the nodule is cancerous and whether surgery is necessary. Papillary carcinoma is the most common type of thyroid cancer, followed by follicular carcinoma, then oncocytic. Papillary, follicular, and oncocytic carcinomas are known as the differentiated thyroid cancers. Differentiated cancers usually grow and spread slowly. Treatment of these types is addressed in Chapter Medullary thyroid cancer is the third most common type of thyroid cancer. This type can be inherited, meaning it can run in families. Medullary thyroid cancer is the focus of Chapter Anaplastic thyroid cancer is the most aggressive type of thyroid cancer. It is rare and most often affects older adults. This type is the focus of Chapter The type and other features of biopsied lesions are recorded in a pathology report. Ask for a copy of the report to have for your records. Your care team uses it to plan the next steps of care. Key points Although most nodules aren't cancerous, a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) test and ultrasound are recommended if a thyroid nodule is known or suspected. Your provider uses the ultrasound results to determine whether a needle biopsy is needed. Biopsy samples are sent to a pathologist. The pathologist determines whether the nodule is cancerous and, if so, the cancer type. 3 Treatments 13 15 16 18 19 21 Surgery Radioactive iodine Radiation therapy Systemic therapy Clinical trials Key points Surgery is the most common treatment for most thyroid cancers. However, active surveillance may be an option for some very-low-risk cancers. This involves closely monitoring the cancer instead of performing surgery right away. Surgery Surgery is the most effective treatment for thyroid cancer. Surgery may involve removing the entire thyroid gland, or just the half that contains cancer. Lobectomy A lobectomy removes the lobe of the thyroid that contains the cancerous nodule. The tissue connecting the two lobes (the isthmus) is also removed. While under general anesthesia, a small incision is made in the front of the neck to remove the cancerous lobe. Lobectomy may be an option for some small and low-risk differentiated thyroid cancers. Total thyroidectomy A total thyroidectomy removes the entire thyroid gland. Lymph nodes near the thyroid are also removed if they are known or suspected to have cancer. This is called a neck dissection. While under general anesthesia, a small incision is made in the front of the neck to remove the gland. Most people stay in the hospital overnight after surgery. After being discharged, it is important to follow the instructions for at-home care. Contact your care team about any new or worsening side effects. Long-term side effects of removing the thyroid can include: Low levels of calcium in the blood (hypoparathyroidism) Damage to the nerves that control your voice and swallowing Thyroid hormone replacement therapy After a total thyroidectomy, medicine is used to replace the hormones no longer being supplied by the thyroid. This is called thyroid hormone replacement therapy. It is needed lifelong in all people after total thyroidectomy. After a lobectomy, about 1 in 3 people need thyroid hormone therapy. Levothyroxine (eg, Levoxyl; Synthroid) is the most commonly used thyroid hormone replacement therapy. The goal for most people is to keep the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the low normal range. For higher risk thyroid cancers, or if there are signs of recurrence, the TSH level is kept lower than the normal range (suppressed). This helps prevent thyroid cancer cells from growing or returning. Suppression is an important part of cancer therapy for most differentiated thyroid cancers.

Immunotherapy is a form of cancer treatment that leverages the body's own immune system to identify, target, and destroy cancer cells. It is classified as a systemic therapy, meaning it works throughout the body, and functions by either stimulating or re-activating the immune system's natural defenses against tumors. This approach can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments, and its application spans various cancer types, including recurrent ovarian cancer, advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, metastatic thyroid cancer, and primary CNS lymphoma, where the monoclonal antibody rituximab is a key agent.

A prominent and often preferred method within immunotherapy involves the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors, which include drugs that target proteins such as PD-1 and PD-L1. A specific example of this class is pembrolizumab. These inhibitors are frequently utilized in clinical practice, particularly for cancers like metastatic anal cancer, where they serve as a primary treatment or are recommended when the disease progresses during or after chemotherapy. In some cases, such as progressive anal cancer, these inhibitors may be administered before surgery. Additionally, immunotherapy can be delivered directly into the bladder for certain malignancies.

The application of immunotherapy is sometimes guided by the presence of specific biomarkers to determine patient eligibility. While it offers a powerful mechanism for fighting cancer, it is not without side effects. Potential adverse reactions include autoimmune responses, fatigue, fever, nausea, loss of appetite, infection, diarrhea, and constipation. Overall, immunotherapy represents a versatile and increasingly central strategy in oncology, offering options for both early and advanced-stage diseases across a wide spectrum of cancer types.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

Surgery is a broad medical term for procedures that involve physical intervention, typically through an incision, to treat disease, remove cancer or other tissue, or repair the body. In oncology, it is a fundamental treatment modality used to physically remove tumors, cancerous tissue, and sometimes nearby lymph nodes. As a treatment for various cancers, its application and feasibility depend on the cancer type, stage, and location. For instance, it is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer and a primary treatment for early-stage cervical cancer, often involving the removal of cancerous tissue. For ovarian cancer, surgery is frequently the initial treatment, often performed by a gynecologic oncologist, and is typically followed by chemotherapy and maintenance therapy; its success depends on tumor size and location. In prostate cancer, surgery involves removing the cancerous tissue, which may include the tumor or the entire prostate, and is an option even for advanced stages. For bladder cancer, the procedure can range from removing the tumor to removing the entire bladder, depending on the stage, and may also involve removing surrounding tissue. In breast cancer, surgery is used as an initial treatment, after which pathologic staging provides more accurate details, and may involve the removal of breast tissue for analysis.

Surgery is also a key treatment for several other malignancies. It is a treatment option for early or locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and for some people with stage 1, 2, or 3 pancreatic cancer to remove cancer from the body. For thyroid cancer, it is a standard treatment involving the physical removal of tissue, with targeted therapy used when surgery cannot be performed. It is a main treatment for glioma, involving tumor removal, and can be the sole treatment for grade 1 gliomas. For chondrosarcoma and other bone cancers, surgery is used to remove tumors. In anal cancer, surgery may be used to remove the anus if the disease does not respond to treatment or returns. However, surgery is not always possible or successful, such as for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), and it is not normally an option for primary CNS lymphoma due to associated risks. Additionally, surgery may have increased side effects for smokers, and staging after the procedure provides more accurate details about the disease.

question: Why is lobectomy preferred over total thyroidectomy for some small, low-risk differentiated thyroid cancers?
ground_truth: Lobectomy is preferred because it is sufficient for small, noninvasive tumors and avoids the need for lifelong thyroid hormone replacement.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. For certain conditions, such as mediastinal gray zone lymphoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer, it is a common or necessary treatment, though it is not highly effective against most thyroid cancers. In stem cell rescue procedures, high-dose chemotherapy is used to destroy lymphoma cells and bone marrow stem cells. Specific drug examples include platinum-based agents like cisplatin and carboplatin, as well as capecitabine and paclitaxel.

Because chemotherapy targets all fast-dividing cells, it can also harm healthy cells, leading to side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fever, infection, tingling or numbness, and rash. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility, as the treatment can affect fertility. Chemotherapy is considered a non-hormone therapy and is a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment, though its effectiveness and side effects depend on the specific drugs used and the individual patient's condition.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Blood Tests are laboratory procedures performed on samples of blood to evaluate a patient’s overall health, detect abnormalities, and assess organ function. These medical tests are frequently documented in medical records and binders, serving as a foundational tool for diagnosing and monitoring a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. By analyzing blood components and chemicals, these tests can reveal signs of disease, measure how well organs are working, and identify specific markers or irregularities that guide clinical decision-making.

In the context of oncology, Blood Tests play a critical role across multiple cancer types. They are routine in cases of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), where results may be abnormal, and are integral to the diagnostic workup for esophageal cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma, where results help guide treatment plans. For suspected ovarian cancer, tests typically include a complete blood count (CBC), chemistry profile, liver function tests, and tumor marker tests. Similarly, for pancreatic cancer, these tests aid in diagnosis and management, while for primary CNS lymphoma, they help assess the condition. In leukemias like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), blood tests are used to diagnose, monitor, and direct treatment strategies. For thyroid cancer, they measure specific substances such as TSH, thyroglobulin (Tg), and Tg antibodies to track disease status.

Beyond initial diagnosis, Blood Tests are essential for ongoing patient care. They are ordered as needed to monitor health and cancer status during chemotherapy, and they help establish the extent of cancer spread for treatment planning. Specific tests, including CBC, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and liver function tests, are used to check for cancer recurrence and to evaluate organ function over time. Additionally, these tests are part of general health checks and are crucial for diagnosing and planning treatment for liver cancer. Overall, Blood Tests provide objective data on blood markers and health indicators, making them indispensable for detecting disease, assessing organ performance, and guiding therapeutic decisions across numerous medical scenarios.

A pathologist is a medical professional and physician expert who specializes in diagnosing diseases, particularly cancer, by examining cells and tissues. They analyze biopsy samples, tissue samples, and other specimens—such as lymph node, bone marrow, and urine samples—under a microscope to detect abnormal cells, confirm the presence of cancer, and determine tumor type, subtype, histology, and grade. This involves comparing cancer cells to normal cells to assess cancer characteristics and assign specific grading systems, such as Gleason patterns for prostate cancer. Pathologists also examine removed tissue to determine cancer stage and test lymph nodes for cancer spread. As part of a multidisciplinary care team, they analyze cells, tissues, and organs removed during biopsies or surgeries, providing essential diagnostic information, staging, and biomarker testing results. They compile their findings into a pathology report, which guides treatment decisions. Their role is critical in confirming cancer diagnoses, identifying tumor subtypes, and evaluating disease progression across various cancer types, including ovarian cancer.

Question:What steps are necessary to diagnose and fully characterize an AML case with suspected extramedullary involvement?
Answer: Based on the supplied context, the necessary steps are:

- **Blood tests** and **bone marrow aspirate and biopsy** to confirm the AML diagnosis.
- **FDG-PET/CT** when leukemia outside the blood and bone marrow (extramedullary disease) is suspected.
- **Biopsy** of the affected tissue, analyzed by a **pathologist/hematopathologist**, to confirm extramedullary involvement.
- **Imaging studies** to guide treatment planning.
- **Biomarker testing** (molecular testing) on the biopsy sample to identify gene mutations or other molecular features.
- Evaluation by a **multidisciplinary team** to plan and implement treatment.

Note: The context does not provide a complete, step-by-step diagnostic algorithm for fully characterizing extramedullary AML, so some details may be insufficient.

entities.description: Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Detection and risk assessment involve various tests, including PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, biopsy, and grading, and the disease often requires staging and treatment. The condition is also a focus of risk assessment and genetic testing discussions, as it is characterized by the presence of prostate cancer cells and abnormal cell growth within the gland.

Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. For certain conditions, such as mediastinal gray zone lymphoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer, it is a common or necessary treatment, though it is not highly effective against most thyroid cancers. In stem cell rescue procedures, high-dose chemotherapy is used to destroy lymphoma cells and bone marrow stem cells. Specific drug examples include platinum-based agents like cisplatin and carboplatin, as well as capecitabine and paclitaxel.

Because chemotherapy targets all fast-dividing cells, it can also harm healthy cells, leading to side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fever, infection, tingling or numbness, and rash. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility, as the treatment can affect fertility. Chemotherapy is considered a non-hormone therapy and is a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment, though its effectiveness and side effects depend on the specific drugs used and the individual patient's condition.

Immunotherapy is a form of cancer treatment that leverages the body's own immune system to identify, target, and destroy cancer cells. It is classified as a systemic therapy, meaning it works throughout the body, and functions by either stimulating or re-activating the immune system's natural defenses against tumors. This approach can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments, and its application spans various cancer types, including recurrent ovarian cancer, advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, metastatic thyroid cancer, and primary CNS lymphoma, where the monoclonal antibody rituximab is a key agent.

A prominent and often preferred method within immunotherapy involves the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors, which include drugs that target proteins such as PD-1 and PD-L1. A specific example of this class is pembrolizumab. These inhibitors are frequently utilized in clinical practice, particularly for cancers like metastatic anal cancer, where they serve as a primary treatment or are recommended when the disease progresses during or after chemotherapy. In some cases, such as progressive anal cancer, these inhibitors may be administered before surgery. Additionally, immunotherapy can be delivered directly into the bladder for certain malignancies.

The application of immunotherapy is sometimes guided by the presence of specific biomarkers to determine patient eligibility. While it offers a powerful mechanism for fighting cancer, it is not without side effects. Potential adverse reactions include autoimmune responses, fatigue, fever, nausea, loss of appetite, infection, diarrhea, and constipation. Overall, immunotherapy represents a versatile and increasingly central strategy in oncology, offering options for both early and advanced-stage diseases across a wide spectrum of cancer types.

Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Common side effects after anal cancer treatment, including fecal incontinence, increased bowel movements, gas, urgency, and watery stool.<SEP>Alterations in bowel function that can occur after anal cancer treatment.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.
A factor considered when choosing bladder cancer treatment.

Medical History is a comprehensive record of a patient's past and current health information, encompassing all health issues, illnesses, injuries, symptoms, treatments, and medications a person has experienced throughout their life. This record serves as a foundational tool for healthcare providers, informing the care team about the patient's overall health status and guiding clinical decision-making. It is actively used to determine the best course of treatment for a patient, including in specific diagnostic contexts such as the evaluation of basal cell skin cancer. The information contained within a medical history is typically gathered during a medical consultation and may also include the health history of close blood relatives, providing a broader context for the patient's health. Ultimately, this detailed review of a patient's past and present health conditions is essential for informing medical decisions and ensuring appropriate, personalized care.

Colon cancer is a disease characterized by the growth of malignant cells in the colon, a part of the large intestine. It is a distinct form of cancer with treatment approaches that differ from those used for rectal cancer. The disease commonly originates from polyps, particularly adenomatous polyps, which are abnormal growths on the inner lining of the colon that can become cancerous over time. Colon cancer is considered a common and treatable form of cancer, especially when detected early, and it can present in various stages, including stages 1, 2, and 3, as well as in non-metastatic or metastatic forms.

The condition may be linked to family history, suggesting a potential genetic or hereditary component that can increase an individual's risk. Additionally, research indicates that having colon cancer may be associated with an elevated risk of developing prostate cancer. As a disease, colon cancer involves the uncontrolled division of abnormal cells within the colon, and its progression and severity are typically classified by staging systems that help guide prognosis and treatment decisions.

Head And Neck Cancer is a broad and diverse category of malignancies that arise in the squamous cells lining the mucosal surfaces of the head and neck region. This group encompasses cancers of the oral cavity (including the mouth, jaw, teeth, and gums), the pharynx (throat), the larynx (voice box), and associated glands. As a broader classification, it includes specific subtypes such as throat cancer. The primary risk factors for developing these cancers include the use of tobacco and alcohol, though a subset of these cancers is also caused by the Human Papillomavirus (HPV).

The disease and its treatment can have significant impacts on a patient's quality of life, potentially affecting the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, and may necessitate dental work prior to the initiation of treatment. Head And Neck Cancer is a broad and diverse category of malignancies that arise in the squamous cells lining the mucosal surfaces of the head and neck region. This group encompasses cancers of the oral cavity (including the mouth, jaw, teeth, and gums), the pharynx (throat), the larynx (voice box), and associated glands. As a broader classification, it includes specific subtypes such as throat cancer. The primary risk factors for developing these cancers include the use of tobacco and alcohol, though a subset of these cancers is also caused by the Human Papillomavirus (HPV).

The disease and its treatment can have significant impacts on a patient's quality of life, potentially affecting the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, and may necessitate dental work prior to the initiation of treatment. Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

entities.description: Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

These medical tests are frequently documented in medical records and binders, serving as a foundational tool for diagnosing and monitoring a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. By analyzing blood components and chemicals, these tests can reveal signs of disease, measure how well organs are working, and identify specific markers or irregularities that guide clinical decision-making.

Cancer Stage is a medical classification that describes the extent of cancer in the body, often written with Roman numerals (e.g., I, II, III, IV). It serves as a standardized assessment of how far the cancer has likely spread from its original site, such as the ovary, and is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment plan for a patient. The staging system categorizes the disease based on whether cancer has remained localized or has metastasized; specifically, stages I, II, and III are considered non-metastatic, indicating that the cancer is confined to the primary site or has spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes, while stage IV denotes metastatic cancer, meaning it has spread to distant organs or parts of the body. This classification provides a clear framework for healthcare providers to evaluate the severity of the disease, guide therapeutic decisions, and communicate the prognosis, ensuring that the treatment approach is tailored to the specific progression of the cancer.

Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Blood is a specialized bodily fluid and tissue that circulates throughout the body, playing essential roles in transporting oxygen and nutrients to cells while carrying away metabolic waste products. It is composed of plasma and formed elements, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Beyond transport, blood is integral to the immune system, defending against pathogens, and to hemostasis, preventing bleeding through clotting mechanisms. Blood also serves as a conduit for hormones, facilitating endocrine signaling, and can be a vehicle for the spread of cancer cells during metastasis, as seen in conditions like liver cancer.

In clinical and diagnostic contexts, blood is a versatile sample source. It is used for genetic testing, including mutation and predisposition testing, as well as tumor marker tests. For certain procedures, such as karyotyping, a blood sample (or bone marrow) is required because it provides living cells that can be cultured and grown. Blood is also a critical medium for monitoring hematologic malignancies; for instance, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), it may contain an accumulation of immature blasts, while in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the overproduction of lymphoblasts can crowd out normal blood cell production. Additionally, blood can harbor cancer cells or circulating tumor DNA, making it a key specimen for liquid biopsies. In therapeutic contexts, blood is a source for harvesting stem cells, which can be used in transplantation and regenerative treatments.

Lymphoblasts are immature white blood cells that normally mature into lymphocytes. In the context of disease, they are most notably associated with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), where they are produced in excess and accumulate in the bone marrow, crowding out normal bone marrow cells and other blood cells. A diagnosis of ALL typically requires the presence of 20% or more lymphoblasts in the bone marrow. Additionally, lymphoblasts can be increased in the blast phase of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), where they appear as a type of blast cell. These cells are considered abnormal when present in elevated numbers, reflecting their role as immature precursors in leukemic conditions.

Myeloblasts are immature blood cells that originate from myeloid progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Under normal conditions, they are very immature white blood cells that mature into non-lymphoid blood cells, specifically differentiating into granulocytes (such as neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils) or monocytes. As a type of blast cell, they represent an early stage in the myeloid cell lineage.

In pathological contexts, myeloblasts play a central role in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). In AML, these immature white blood cells become abnormal and accumulate in the bone marrow and blood, preventing normal blood cell production and function. Similarly, myeloblasts are identified as a type of blast cell involved in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), where their presence reflects disrupted myeloid maturation. Across these conditions, the key characteristic of myeloblasts is their immaturity and their failure to undergo normal differentiation, leading to their accumulation and impairment of healthy hematopoiesis.

Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

Blood is a specialized bodily fluid and tissue that circulates throughout the body, playing essential roles in transporting oxygen and nutrients to cells while carrying away metabolic waste products. It is composed of plasma and formed elements, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Beyond transport, blood is integral to the immune system, defending against pathogens, and to hemostasis, preventing bleeding through clotting mechanisms. Blood also serves as a conduit for hormones, facilitating endocrine signaling, and can be a vehicle for the spread of cancer cells during metastasis, as seen in conditions like liver cancer.

In clinical and diagnostic contexts, blood is a versatile sample source. It is used for genetic testing, including mutation and predisposition testing, as well as tumor marker tests. For certain procedures, such as karyotyping, a blood sample (or bone marrow) is required because it provides living cells that can be cultured and grown. Blood is also a critical medium for monitoring hematologic malignancies; for instance, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), it may contain an accumulation of immature blasts, while in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the overproduction of lymphoblasts can crowd out normal blood cell production. Additionally, blood can harbor cancer cells or circulating tumor DNA, making it a key specimen for liquid biopsies. In therapeutic contexts, blood is a source for harvesting stem cells, which can be used in transplantation and regenerative treatments.

Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are a comprehensive set of patient-friendly guidelines published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), a nonprofit alliance of leading cancer centers. These guidelines translate the expert consensus of the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology into plain-language explanations, designed to help people with cancer, their families, and caregivers understand current care recommendations. The guidelines are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers, providing trusted, up-to-date information on cancer treatment, testing, staging, and side effects.

These resources cover a wide range of cancer types, including squamous cell skin cancer, melanoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, anal cancer, bone cancer, and certain lymphomas, as well as topics like adolescent and young adult cancer. They also address specific concerns such as immunotherapy side effects and fertility and family planning for cancer patients. The guidelines aim to empower patients to make informed, shared decisions with their care team by clearly explaining their treatment options and what to expect.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are accessible in multiple formats, including online at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and through the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. They are also available as printed books. The NCCN encourages users to provide feedback through surveys to help improve the guidelines. Overall, these guidelines serve as a vital educational resource, bridging the gap between complex medical information and patient understanding, ensuring individuals are well-informed participants in their own cancer care journey.

Myeloblasts are immature blood cells that originate from myeloid progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Under normal conditions, they are very immature white blood cells that mature into non-lymphoid blood cells, specifically differentiating into granulocytes (such as neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils) or monocytes. In AML, these immature white blood cells become abnormal and accumulate in the bone marrow and blood, preventing normal blood cell production and function. Similarly, myeloblasts are identified as a type of blast cell involved in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), where their presence reflects disrupted myeloid maturation. Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Biomarker Testing is a medical procedure used in oncology that analyzes biological molecules—such as DNA mutations, proteins, or other molecular features—found in tumor tissue, biopsy samples, or blood to inform cancer care. Also known as molecular testing or tumor profiling, it is performed to identify specific genetic alterations or protein expressions that indicate the presence or progression of cancer, thereby aiding in diagnosis and prognosis. The testing examines genes or their products to detect mutations and proteins that may suggest effective treatment options, helping to guide decisions on whether a patient is eligible for targeted therapies or immunotherapies.

The scope of biomarker testing is broad, encompassing various cancer types and specific markers. For instance, it is used to guide diagnosis and treatment in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and to assess risk and aggressiveness in prostate cancer by examining molecular components of biopsy samples. Common biomarkers tested include hormone receptors, HER2, PD-L1, MMR, MSI, TMB, NTRK, RET, p16, and EBV DNA, among others. These tests help determine the presence of specific biological markers that can predict response to particular drugs, thereby fine-tuning treatment plans and improving diagnostic accuracy.

Biomarker testing can be performed on tumor tissue or through liquid biopsies of blood, depending on the clinical need. The results provide critical information on the molecular profile of the cancer, enabling healthcare providers to select the most appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach. By identifying actionable mutations or protein levels, this testing plays a central role in precision medicine, ensuring that patients receive treatments most likely to be effective while avoiding unnecessary interventions.
